Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
As a forester, 54-year-old Jack had spent his career navigating the rugged terrain of the Pacific Northwest. He knew every inch of those woods, every hidden stream and every ancient tree. But it was on one of those familiar trails that Jack's life changed forever. He was leading a team of loggers when a felled tree unexpectedly rolled down the hill, crushing one of his coworkers beneath its massive trunk. Jack had given the order to fell the tree, and in that instant, he knew he had made a terrible mistake. The memory of that day still seared itself into Jack's mind like a branding iron. He could smell the sap and sweat, feel the cool mist on his skin, and see the look of terror in his coworker's eyes as the tree came crashing down. When those memories surfaced – and they did so frequently – Jack's body would contort into the same position it had been in that day, as if trying to relive the moment, to undo what had been done. He'd feel a surge of rage, too, directed at himself, at his own carelessness. How could he have been so reckless? The grief that followed was suffocating, threatening to consume him whole. In the months following the accident, Jack found it increasingly difficult to relax, even in the safety of his own home. His mind was always on high alert, scanning for potential dangers, convinced that another disaster lurked just around the corner. Strangers, especially men with a rugged outdoorsy look, made him uneasy – their approach would send Jack's heart racing as he searched for signs of hostility. He began to watch people closely, trying to read their intentions before they could pose a threat. Physical pain, too, had become a potent trigger. A twinge in his shoulder or a sharp ache in his back would transport Jack right back to that fateful day. His body was a map of vulnerabilities, each one tracing back to the moment when he'd lost control. He started avoiding activities that brought him physical discomfort, even going so far as to turn down logging jobs that required heavy lifting or strenuous labor. As the weeks turned into months, Jack's life began to narrow. He withdrew from his colleagues and friends, afraid of being reminded of what had happened. His wife, Sarah, tried to be supportive, but Jack couldn't shake the feeling that he was a danger to those around him – that some fundamental flaw in his character had led to the accident. He became convinced that he was no longer capable of doing the work that defined him as a forester and a man. The physical proximity of others also began to unnerve Jack. Being in crowded spaces or surrounded by people would send his anxiety spiking. He started taking long, solo drives through the woods, trying to escape the sense of vulnerability that seemed to cling to him like a shroud. It was Sarah who finally convinced Jack to seek help. She pointed out how much he'd changed – how withdrawn and isolated he'd become – and expressed her own fears for his well-being. As Jack sat in the therapist's office, recounting the events of that terrible day and the months that followed, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was staring into an abyss. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves but what they seemed to reveal about himself – that he was a man who could cause harm, even when he least intended it. For Jack, seeking help felt like a last resort, a desperate attempt to reclaim some semblance of his former life. He hoped that therapy might somehow repair the damage done, not just to others but to his own sense of self. As he looked back on the events that had brought him here, Jack couldn't help but wonder if he'd ever be able to find peace again – or if the forest, once a sanctuary, would forever hold the echoes of that terrible day.
